notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Ezekiel 4, drawn from the pages I was able to fetch and read.

---

## Ezekiel 4 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Overview / Structure

The chapter contains four symbolic acted-out prophecies: (1) the clay-brick siege model (vv. 1–3), (2) lying on left and right sides to bear iniquity (vv. 4–8), (3) the rationed defiled bread (vv. 9–13), and (4) God's accommodation to Ezekiel's objection (vv. 14–17). A long-standing question among commentators is whether these signs were literally performed or were visionary. Dummelow says, "It is uncertain whether these actions were literally performed or not … some of those in Ezekiel 4 are so extraordinary that many suppose that they were not actually carried out, but only imagined and described" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/ezekiel-4.html). Ellicott similarly suggests it "is more likely that he simply described, rather than actually performed, these symbolical acts" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/4.htm). JFB thinks the second action (vv. 4–8) was "in vision, not in external action, wherein it would have been only puerile" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/4.htm). Guzik (Enduring Word), however, treats them as actual public performances: "These daily public acts were not private meditation but witnessed community theater" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-4/).

---

### v. 1 — The Clay Brick

**"Now you, son of man, take a brick, place it before you, and draw on it the city of Jerusalem."**

- **Ellicott** notes that the use of tiles for writing/drawing was common in both Babylonia and Nineveh: clay was inscribed while soft, then baked. Great libraries were preserved this way (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/4.htm).
- **JFB** adds that the tile was "a sun-dried brick, such as are found in Babylon, covered with cuneiform inscriptions, often two feet long and one foot broad" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/4.htm).
- **Guzik** (Enduring Word) cites Feinberg: "The tile mentioned in the text was a tablet of soft clay, baked to make it durable, such as the Babylonians used for writing purposes." He also cites Block noting that archaeologists have found a 2nd-millennium plan of Nippur on a clay brick, confirming the practice (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-4/).
- **Dummelow**: the brick was "a slab of clay, such as the Babylonians used for inscriptions and sculptures in relief" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/ezekiel-4.html).

---

### v. 2 — The Mimic Siege

**"Then lay siege against it: Construct a siege wall, build a ramp to it, set up camps against it, and place battering rams around it on all sides."**

- **Ellicott** describes each siege element: first investment; then a watch-tower high enough to overlook the walls and hold throwing engines; then a mound (artificial hill) giving besiegers an elevated position; then camps to prevent ingress/egress; finally battering rams — heavy beams, headed with iron, slung in towers and swung against walls. The ram-shaped head was a later Greek/Roman development, but the instrument itself was much older (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/4.htm).
- **JFB**: "fort" means "watch-tower" (Jer 52:4) where besiegers could watch the besieged. "Battering-rams" literally means "through-borers" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/4.htm).
- **Ellicott** notes the historical irony: at the time Ezekiel prophesied, a fresh siege seemed unlikely. Nebuchadnezzar had already conquered Judah three times, carried two kings captive, and installed Zedekiah as a puppet. Only "simple infatuation" — Zedekiah's rebellion — would bring another siege. Yet "through the 'anger of the LORD' (2 Kings 24:20)" this is exactly what happened. The siege began about four years after this prophecy (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/4.htm).
- **Guzik** (Enduring Word) cites Wiersbe: "This, of course, was what would happen at Jerusalem in 588 B.C. when the Babylonian army began the siege of the city" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-4/).

---

### v. 3 — The Iron Plate

**"Then take an iron plate and set it up as an iron wall between yourself and the city. Turn your face toward it so that it is under siege, and besiege it. This will be a sign to the house of Israel."**

- **Multiple interpretations of the iron plate:**
  - **Guzik** (Enduring Word): "The iron plate Ezekiel placed between himself and the clay city symbolized an unbreakable barrier between God and Jerusalem — God would not intervene to save the city when Babylon came" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-4/). He cites Wiersbe: it was the kind of griddle priests used in the temple (Lev 2:5; 6:21; 7:9), and "symbolized the wall that stood between God and the sinful Jewish nation."
  - **Ellicott**: "doubtless as symbolical of the strength of the besiegers' lines, and of the impossibility there would be of an escape from the city by a sally. Their foes should be made too strong for them defensively as well as offensively" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/4.htm). The "iron pan" (margin: "flat plate") was the type used for baking cakes.
  - **Dummelow** gives three possibilities: "a symbol either of the stubbornness of the defence or of the rigour of the siege. Or it may represent the hopeless barrier which now separated God from His people" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/ezekiel-4.html).
  - **JFB**: the iron pan represents "the divine decree as to the Chaldean army investing the city … His instrument of separating them from him, as one impossible to burst through" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/4.htm).
- **Gill**: the iron pan "seems to represent all such things as are made use of by besiegers to screen them from the besieged; such as are now used are trenches, parapets, bastions, &c." (from search excerpt).

---

### v. 4 — Lying on the Left Side

**"Then lie down on your left side and place the iniquity of the house of Israel upon yourself. You are to bear their iniquity for the number of days you lie on your side."**

- **"Left side" symbolism**: Because Orientals faced east when determining directions, the north was on the left. Israel (the northern kingdom of the ten tribes) therefore corresponds to the left side (Ellicott, JFB, Dummelow). JFB adds that the right side was more honourable, fitting Judah as the seat of the temple (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/4.htm).
- **"Bear their iniquity"** means to bear the *punishment* of their sin, not to atone for it. Ellicott says, "The expression, to bear the iniquity of any one, is common in Scripture to denote the suffering of the punishment due to sin" — citing Ezek 18:19–20; Lev 19:8; Num 14:34; Isa 53:12 (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/4.htm). JFB notes this was "A type of Him who was the great sin-bearer, not in mimic show as Ezekiel, but in reality (Isa 53:4, 6, 12)" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/4.htm).
- **Guzik** (Enduring Word) cites Block: "He now plays the role of the priest, carrying the burden of his people's sins on his shoulder" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-4/).
- **Guzik** also cites Taylor for a geographical detail: the prophet probably lay east-west, head toward Jerusalem, facing north on his left side (toward Israel) and south on his right side (toward Judah) (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-4/).

---

### v. 5 — The 390 Days

**"For I have assigned to you 390 days, according to the number of years of their iniquity. So you shall bear the iniquity of the house of Israel."**

This is one of the most debated numbers in Ezekiel.

- **Ellicott's Excursus** surveys many interpretations and finds them all wanting. The interpretation he endorses (as "now generally given by the best modern expositors") is that Ezekiel is deliberately echoing Numbers 14:34 ("each day for a year shall ye bear your iniquities") and using the numbers typologically: Israel's exile is being depicted as a new Egyptian bondage. The 430 years of the Egyptian sojourn (Ex 12:40) minus the 40 years of wilderness wandering = 390. So "No precise period whatever is intended by the mention of these numbers, but only a vivid comparison of the future woes to the past" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/4.htm).
- **JFB** (Fairbairn) takes the same approach: "The sum of three hundred ninety and forty years is four hundred thirty, a period famous in the history of the covenant-people, being that of their sojourn in Egypt … God will reduce them to a kind of new Egyptian bondage to the world." JFB also suggests a literal reckoning: 390 years from Jeroboam's setting up of the calves (975 BC) to about the year of the Babylonian captivity (583 BC) (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/4.htm).
- **Guzik** (Enduring Word) prefers the calculation of the kings of Judah: adding the reigns from Rehoboam to Zedekiah (1–2 Kings) totals about 394 years; subtract the three years Rehoboam walked with God (2 Chron 11:16–17) = about 390 (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-4/).
- **Dummelow** notes the LXX reads 190 instead of 390. If 190 is correct, the difference between the two captivities becomes about 150 years, which fits the historical gap between the fall of Samaria (721 BC) and the first captivity (597 BC) as a round number (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/ezekiel-4.html).
- **Guzik** also notes Feinberg's insistence that "Ezekiel 4:4 makes it plain that the period must not represent the time of Israel's sinning, but the period during which the nation bears its iniquity and is punished" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-4/).

---

### v. 6 — The 40 Days for Judah

**"When you have completed these days, lie down again, but on your right side, and bear the iniquity of the house of Judah. I have assigned to you 40 days, a day for each year."**

- **Ellicott**: The great disproportion between Israel's 390 (or 190 in LXX) and Judah's 40 "is in accordance with the difference in the two parts of the nation." Judah kept the Davidic line, the temple, and the Aaronic priesthood, and had several devout kings; Israel had no godly king, made Baal the national god, and set up a false priesthood (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/4.htm).
- **JFB**: "Forty alludes to the forty years in the wilderness" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/4.htm).
- **Dummelow**: 40 is either from Numbers 14:34 or is simply "a round number, meaning 'more than a generation'" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/ezekiel-4.html).
- **Ellicott**: The two periods are "clearly subsequent and additional," making 430 total. The days represent years. The period is one of *bearing* (suffering) punishment, not of *accumulating* sin (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/4.htm).

---

### v. 7 — Bared Arm and Prophesying

**"You must turn your face toward the siege of Jerusalem with your arm bared, and prophesy against it."**

- **"Set thy face"**: Ellicott calls this "a common Scriptural expression for any steadfast purpose" and a favourite phrase of Ezekiel (Ezek 15:7; 20:46, etc.). It signifies God's unrelenting purpose of judgment (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/4.htm).
- **"Arm shall be uncovered"**: The loose sleeve of the Oriental robe was withdrawn to make the arm ready for battle (Ellicott, referencing Isa 52:10). Guzik cites Poole: "Thine arm, thy right arm, the stronger and more ready to act, shall be uncovered, naked and stretched out, as being ready to strike and slay" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-4/). JFB: "to be ready for action, which the long Oriental garment usually covering it would prevent" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/4.htm).
- **Dummelow** simply calls it "a threatening gesture" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/ezekiel-4.html).
- **Gill**: "and thou shall prophesy against it: meaning not so much by words, if at all, but by these actions, gestures, and habit; for they all foretold what would certainly come to pass" (from search excerpt).

---

### v. 8 — Bound with Ropes

**"Now behold, I will tie you up with ropes so you cannot turn from side to side until you have finished the days of your siege."**

- **Ellicott**: "This is a fresh feature of the unrelenting character of the judgment foretold: God's power should interpose to keep the prophet to his work. Not only pity, but even human weakness and weariness, should be excluded from interfering" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/4.htm).
- **JFB**: The bands signify "the impossibility of their being able to shake off the punishment" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/4.htm).
- **Guzik** (Enduring Word): "After symbolically standing in the place of God, Ezekiel then stood in the place of Jerusalem, restrained and helpless before God and His coming judgment." He also notes Feinberg's comment: "It is not necessary to assume that Ezekiel was in the prone position day and night. It was doubtless part of each day" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-4/).
- **Dummelow**: "By some divine restraint Ezekiel would be prevented from turning." He notes the days of siege also total 430, though the actual siege of Jerusalem "lasted almost exactly a year and a half (2 Kings 25:1–3; Jer 39:1–2)" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/ezekiel-4.html).
- **Gill**: This shows "that the Chaldean army should not depart from Jerusalem until it was taken" (from search excerpt).

---

### v. 9 — The Mixed-Grain Bread

**"But take wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet, and spelt; put them in a single container and make them into bread for yourself. This is what you are to eat during the 390 days you lie on your side."**

- **Gill**: Wheat was the normal bread grain; barley was used in poverty; the rest (beans, lentils, millet, spelt) were normally animal fodder, "never used for the food of men but in a time of great scarcity; wherefore this was designed to denote the famine that should attend the siege of Jerusalem" (from search excerpt).
- **JFB**: "Instead of simple flour used for delicate cakes (Gen 18:6), the Jews should have a coarse mixture of six different kinds of grain, such as the poorest alone would eat" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/4.htm).
- **Ellicott**: Mixing diverse grains in one vessel, while perhaps not against the exact letter of the law, was "a plain violation of its spirit (Lev 19:19; Deut 22:9), thus again indicating the stern necessity which should be laid upon the people" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/4.htm).
- **Guzik** (Enduring Word) cites Clarke: "In times of scarcity, it is customary in all countries to mix several kinds of coarser grain with the finer, to make it last the longer" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-4/).
- **Guzik** also notes that the 390-day period for eating this bread shows Ezekiel "was not completely inactive and lying on his side continually" — he was preparing and eating food (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-4/).
- **Dummelow**: "a mixture of all sorts of grain, fine and coarse, symbolising the poor fare which would be used in Jerusalem during the siege" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/ezekiel-4.html).

---

### vv. 10–11 — Rationed Food and Water

**"You are to weigh out twenty shekels of food to eat each day … You are also to measure out a sixth of a hin of water to drink …"**

- **Guzik** (Enduring Word), citing Taylor: "With a shekel calculated at about 11.4 grammes, this would amount to almost exactly 8 ounces of bread per day. The water measurement of one-sixth of a hin would be equal to a fraction over a pint, or 0.61 litres." He adds Poole's comment: "Scarce enough to keep the man alive. Such proportions of bread and water rather fed death than the man" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-4/).
- **Ellicott**: twenty shekels = "something less than eleven ounces, scarcely enough to sustain life." The water = from six-tenths to nine-tenths of a pint, also once a day. The weighing (rather than measuring) of food denotes extreme scarcity. "'From time to time' means at set intervals of time … here doubtless once a day" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/4.htm).
- **Dummelow**: twenty shekels = "eight or nine ounces"; the sixth of a hin = "less than a quart" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/ezekiel-4.html).
- **JFB**: twenty shekels = "little more than ten ounces; a scant measure to sustain life (Jer 52:6). But it applies not only to the siege, but to their whole subsequent state" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/4.htm).

---

### v. 12 — Baking Over Human Dung

**"And you shall eat the food as you would a barley cake, after you bake it over dried human excrement in the sight of the people."**

- **Guzik** (Enduring Word) makes an important clarification via Feinberg: "Some have wholly misunderstood the command of Ezekiel 4:12 which relates only to the *fuel* to prepare the food and not to the making of the food itself." The dung was for the fire, not an ingredient in the bread. Guzik also cites Vawter and Hoppe: "There is no recorded prohibition in the kashrut ('kosher') laws of the Torah regarding the use of human excrement for fuel." He adds Wright's point: "Dried animal dung was used as fuel in the east, and still is, and it was not regarded as ritually unclean. However, in the siege all cattle would be killed for food, so only human excrement would be available for fuel" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-4/).
- **Ellicott**: barley cakes were "commonly cooked in the hot ashes, hence the especial defilement caused by the fuel required to be used" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/4.htm).
- **JFB**: "To use human dung … implies the most cruel necessity. It was in violation of the law (Deut 14:3; 23:12–14); it must therefore have been done only in vision" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/4.htm).
- **Gill**: The prophet was to take the dung, dry it, cover the loaves with it, and burn it over them — "which must be a very disagreeable task to him, and make the food very nauseous." This showed "scarcity of fuel, and the severity of the famine; that they had not fuel to bake with" (from search excerpt).
- **Dummelow**: "Bread thus baked would be unclean (Lev 5:3; Lev 7:21)" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/ezekiel-4.html).

---

### v. 13 — The Meaning: Defiled Bread Among the Nations

**"Then the LORD said, 'This is how the Israelites will eat their defiled bread among the nations to which I will banish them.'"**

- **Ellicott** gives the most thorough theological explanation: The Mosaic law so hedged Israel about with food regulations that sharing Gentile food inevitably meant ceremonial defilement. In exile, they would be *forced* into uncleanness. "Their sins had brought them to that pass, which is so often the result of continued and obdurate sin, that it should be impossible for them to avoid further transgression." He also connects this to Hosea 9:3–4, where the food of exiles cannot be consecrated at the temple and is therefore unclean (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/4.htm).
- **The Expositor's Bible Commentary** (from search excerpt) expands on this: the idea is that all food unconsecrated by presentation at the sanctuary is necessarily unclean. "In the very act of satisfying his natural appetite a man forfeits his religious standing." The destruction of the sanctuary reduced the whole life of the people to uncleanness — "as great a calamity as was a papal interdict in the Middle Ages" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ezekiel-4.html).
- **JFB**: "Implying that Israel's peculiar distinction was to be abolished and that they were to be outwardly blended with the idolatrous heathen (Deut 28:68; Hos 9:3)" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/4.htm).
- **Dummelow**: "Foreign lands were regarded as unclean in themselves (Amos 7:17), and, besides, all food eaten in them would be unclean, because it could not be consecrated by offering a portion to God in the Temple: see Hosea 9:3, 4" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/ezekiel-4.html).

---

### v. 14 — Ezekiel's Objection

**"'Ah, Lord GOD,' I said, 'I have never defiled myself. From my youth until now I have not eaten anything found dead or mauled by wild beasts. No unclean meat has ever entered my mouth.'"**

- **Ellicott** notes that Ezekiel, like Peter in Acts 10:14, had been a scrupulous observer of the dietary law. "To St. Peter, however, it was made known that in the breadth of the Christian dispensation this ceremonial law was now done away, while to Ezekiel it still remained in full force" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/4.htm).
- **JFB**: "Ezekiel, as a priest, had been accustomed to the strictest abstinence from everything legally impure." He distinguishes: "Positive precepts, being dependent on a particular command can be set aside at the will of the divine ruler; but moral precepts are everlasting in their obligation because God cannot be inconsistent with His unchanging moral nature" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/4.htm).
- **Guzik** (Enduring Word) notes Ezekiel's objection "was based on the fact that he had never so offensively broken Jewish dietary laws" and cites Trapp: "Let us be as careful of spiritual uncleanness; sin is the devil's excrement, the corruption of a dead soul" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-4/).
- **Dummelow**: "Ezekiel, as a priest, was peculiarly sensitive about ceremonial defilement" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/ezekiel-4.html).
- **The Expositor's Bible Commentary** (from search excerpt): "The repugnance which he feels at the loathsome manner in which he was at first directed to prepare his food, and the profession of his own practice in exile … are all characteristic of one whose priestly training had made a defect of ceremonial cleanness almost equivalent to a moral delinquency" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ezekiel-4.html).

---

### v. 15 — God's Concession: Cow Dung Instead

**"'Look,' He replied, 'I will let you use cow dung instead of human excrement, and you may bake your bread over that.'"**

- **Guzik** (Enduring Word): "God accommodated the appeal of the prophet. The lesson could be made without actually using human waste to bake the bread." He notes Feinberg's point that normally dung was *not* used for baking bread — even animal dung was considered ritually unclean for that purpose. "God allowed Ezekiel to lessen the offense, but not take it away." Guzik also records Meyer's pastoral observation: "We may be feeling that certain trials are insupportable, or certain demands beyond our power to meet. At such hours of bitter anguish it is quite permissible for us to go into the secret place of the Most High and gasp out our complaint" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-4/).
- **Ellicott**: "In the scarcity of fuel in the East, cow's dung and especially camel's dung, is dried, and becomes the common fuel" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/4.htm).
- **JFB**: This is "a mitigation of the former order … still the bread so baked is 'defiled,' to imply that, whatever partial abatement there might be for the prophet's sake, the main decree of God, as to the pollution of Israel by exile among Gentiles, is unalterable" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/4.htm).
- **Dummelow**: "A partial mitigation of the symbol for the prophet's sake … Though the symbol was modified, it was not implied that the defilement of captivity, signified by the fuel first prescribed, would be any the less" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/ezekiel-4.html).

---

### v. 16 — The Plain Interpretation: Famine in Jerusalem

**"Then He told me, 'Son of man, I am going to cut off the supply of food in Jerusalem. They will anxiously eat bread rationed by weight, and in despair they will drink water by measure.'"**

- **"Break the staff of bread"**: JFB explains this as "bread by which life is supported, as a man's weight is by the staff he leans on (Lev 26:26; Ps 105:16; Isa 3:1)" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/4.htm).
- **Gill**: God "would both deprive them of a sufficiency of bread, the nourishment of man; and not suffer the little they had to be nourishing to them; what they ate would not satisfy them" (from search excerpt).
- **Ellicott**: "In Ezekiel 4:16–17, the meaning of the foregoing symbolism is declared in plain language. Bread, as the chief article of food is put for all food, the specific for the general. There shall be extreme suffering and distress, as a part of the punishment for their long-continued sins" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/4.htm).
- **Guzik** (Enduring Word) cites Feinberg: "The purpose of all the acts in symbolic form was to impress the people with the coming famine during the siege of Jerusalem and the people's subsequent pollution in exile among the heathen" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-4/).

---

### v. 17 — Wasting Away in Iniquity

**"So they will lack food and water; they will be appalled at the sight of one another wasting away in their iniquity."**

- **JFB**: "'astonied one with another' — mutually regard one another with astonishment: the stupefied look of despairing want" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/4.htm).
- **Guzik** (Enduring Word) quotes Poole: "Thus their sins would bring them to extremest want and shame" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-4/).
- **Ellicott** does not add specific comment on this verse beyond noting it concludes the plain-language explanation of the symbolism (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/4.htm).

---

## Points Where Traditions Differ

### Literal vs. Visionary Performance
- **Conservative/Evangelical (Guzik/Enduring Word)**: treats the acts as literally performed — public "community theater," with Ezekiel actually baking and eating, explaining daily to neighbours (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-4/).
- **JFB (Reformed-leaning)**: The siege model (vv. 1–3) may have been performed, but vv. 4–8 were "in vision, not in external action, wherein it would have been only puerile" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/4.htm).
- **The Expositor's Bible Commentary (critical/modern)**: "It is clear that these signs could never have been enacted, either in view of the people or in solitude, as they are here described … the whole description is … purely ideal, representing a process which passed through the prophet's mind" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/ezekiel-4.html).

### The 390/40 Days
- **"Typological" view (Ellicott, JFB/Fairbairn)**: The numbers are not literal historical periods but typological echoes of 430 years in Egypt minus 40 years in the wilderness = 390 (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/4.htm; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/4.htm).
- **"Chronological" view (Wiersbe, via Guzik)**: The 390 years correspond to the summed reigns of Judah's kings from Rehoboam to Zedekiah (about 394 years, minus the three good years of Rehoboam) (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-4/).
- **LXX/Text-critical view (Dummelow, many modern scholars)**: The original Hebrew likely read 190 days, which together with 40 makes 230. The 150-year difference (190 – 40) roughly matches the actual gap between the fall of Samaria (721 BC) and the fall of Jerusalem (586 BC) (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/ezekiel-4.html).

### The Iron Plate
- Some see it as God's barrier (Guzik/Wiersbe, JFB), others as a representation of the besiegers' defensive strength (Ellicott), and Dummelow offers all three interpretations as viable (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/ezekiel-4.html).

---
